title: Denis Villeneuve Defends Casting Robert Pattinson as Bond: ‘We Will Never Please Everybody’
summary: "At the end of the day, the truth will be on the screen," the filmmaker says The post Denis Villeneuve Defends Casting Robert Pattinson as Bond: ‘We Will Never Please Everybody’ appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Denis Villeneuve has addressed the inevitable criticism of his choice to cast Robert Pattinson as James Bond , noting on Friday, “No matter what we do, we will never please everybody.” Villeneuve spoke extensively about his newest film, “Dune: Part Three,” as well as his untitled Bond project, in a new interview with Time Magazine . While the interview was conducted prior to Pattinson’s reveal as 007 , Villeneuve predicted there would be a “hurricane” of responses to his decision once it was publicly announced. “When Daniel Craig was cast, it was a s—tstorm. He was blond. He was short. He was not seen as an action hero,” Villeneuve observed. “Yet when we talk about James Bond today it is because of Daniel Craig’s extraordinary interpretation. And that was a different environment in 2006 before social media.” “I expect a hurricane when we bring our choice to the world. Some people will be happy. Some will be mad. I can do nothing about that,” he added. “At the end of the day, the truth will be on the screen. Then they will be able to judge.” Villeneuve also shrugged off a question about the betting markets that had sprouted up in the months preceding his pivotal casting decision. “I read nothing about that. My responsibility is to make the best casting and create the best story for that cast. I cannot listen to the rumors,” he said. “No matter what we do, we will never please everybody.” In the same interview, Villeneuve said he felt like he has “electricity in my veins” ideating about his Bond film, which will be his first project not set in the “Dune” universe since 2017’s “Blade Runner 2049.” He went on to offer some brief insight into what Bond fans should expect from his forthcoming reboot. “I will say: I love traditions. I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache,” Villeneuve said. “I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today.” “I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film,” he continued. “Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure.” Little is known right now about Villeneuve’s Bond project outside of Pattinson’s casting. “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight has been tapped to write the script for the film, which will be the first Bond movie since Craig concluded his acclaimed run as the character in 2021’s “No Time to Die.” The post Denis Villeneuve Defends Casting Robert Pattinson as Bond: ‘We Will Never Please Everybody’ appeared first on TheWrap .

title: Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Has a Post-Credits Scene: Here’s What You Might’ve Missed
summary: It makes good on a promise from earlier in the movie The post Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Has a Post-Credits Scene: Here’s What You Might’ve Missed appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Note: Light spoilers ahead for Disney’s “Hexed” Considering Disney’s “Hexed” is not a Marvel film, you might not have expected to have to stick around for a post-credits scene, but indeed, there is one. The good news is, it doesn’t contain a secret sequel set-up. No, that happens explicitly in the final minutes of the film itself. After defeating the evil queen and completing the Hexe founders’ spell, witches Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) and Alice (Rashida Jones) wonder if there are more witches out there like them, hinting at the formation of a coven. The credits then roll, set to a cover of The Cars’ song “Magic,” by Steinfeld . But, if you stick around for a bit, you’ll be treated to a bonus scene, making good on a promise from earlier in the film. In seeking out help to save her mom, Billie finds herself at the home of Beef Roger Crummchuk (Walton Goggins), her mother’s former familiar. He has a collection of cat figurines that, thanks to her clumsiness, Billie somewhat demolishes. But, she promises to replace the statues that she breaks. The post-credits scene fulfills that vow, finding Billie, Beef and Alice at the store, buying a whole cauldron’s worth of figurines. The checkout guy is, understandably, a bit perturbed at the three-eyed creature and magical bucket, but makes the sale all the same. Upon exiting the store, Beef and the cauldron crash through the glass of the door, so Billie magically multiplies the money in her hand, covering those damages as well. It’s not the most consequential scene in existence, just a fun little bonus you might’ve missed if you popped out of the theater too soon! Disney’s “Hexed” is now in theaters everywhere. title: Amelia Dimoldenberg Cries Through Final ‘Chicken Shop Date’: ‘I’m Ready to Try Something Else’
summary: "I feel now trapped in a cage of my own making," the creator and host says The post Amelia Dimoldenberg Cries Through Final ‘Chicken Shop Date’: ‘I’m Ready to Try Something Else’ appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Amelia Dimoldenberg’s final episode of “Chicken Shop Date” was extra special and extra emotional on Friday, as the creator and host cried through the top of the episode with guest Ester Perel. After announcing the show was coming to an end earlier this year, the last episode dropped with the Belgian relationship therapist. The waterworks came fast as Dimoldenberg explained that she wanted to have a real relationship and was unsure if that was going to be possible with the show running. “I think I have to end the show to meet somebody,” Dimoldenberg said. “I definitely would love to meet someone that wasn’t a celebrity, if I’m being honest. It seems very intense to go out with a celebrity.” Perel told the host to treat their conversation as if Dimoldenberg was talking to the show itself. She wanted to know exactly what she would say to “Chicken Shop Date” as things were ending. “Thank you for allowing me to be where I am today,” Dimoldenberg said, speaking to the show itself. “I’ve learned so much. I’ve grown up so much and I’ve had so much fun. But I feel now trapped in a cage of my own making and I’m ready to try something else. I never thought I would be able to say goodbye. I thought you would be part of my life forever.” She added: “It was quite a shock to realize that doesn’t need to be the case. And now I feel kind of liberated in the farewell, in thinking there could be another path.” Earlier this week, the host of the viral interview series penned an essay for The Cut that laid out exactly why she came to her decision. Largely, it boiled down to how the show was bleeding more into her real life and that line of thinking eventually led to a stretch of panic attacks that had her finally taking a long look at how much longer she was up for doing the show she loved and created. “I knew my perspective on ‘Chicken Shop Date’ was changing around 18 months ago, when I had my first and then second panic attack ever in the space of a week,” Dimoldenberg said. “Granted, the second one was at an insanely overstimulating karaoke bar called the K-Hole, but still, I knew something was up. I had stopped drinking at the time because I was trying to pinpoint exactly why I felt so unlike myself. All of my emotions felt so much more visceral; I figured that’s what happens when you cut out a sedative. I had started seeing a therapist a few months earlier in the hope that they might provide an answer as to why I was feeling so flat, so low, so confused. The last time I felt like this, it led me to break up with a boyfriend. But now I was single, and unfortunately, I couldn’t pin this all to a man who was dragging me down.” She added: “Naturally, questions started coming up around work. I was at the helm of a job I had created for myself — I was in complete control of every aspect of it. For over ten years, I had assembled a show, a brand, an identity with such care and detail — how could it be something I wanted to free myself from? It became clear I was in a relationship more all-consuming and self-defining than any I’d been in previously. But when a relationship must come to an end, your body might tell you first, then your brain. Then you just know. ‘Damn it,’ I thought. ‘I need to break up with “Chicken Shop Date.”’” The post Amelia Dimoldenberg Cries Through Final ‘Chicken Shop Date’: ‘I’m Ready to Try Something Else’ appeared first on TheWrap .

title: Amy Poehler and Tina Fey Roast LA Thanksgivings
summary: Of course they use their best Valley girl voices to do it The post Amy Poehler and Tina Fey Roast LA Thanksgivings appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Depending on where in the country you live, Thanksgiving probably looks pretty different to other people’s. So, on Thursday night, Amy Poehler and Tina Fey took some time out to roast LA Thanksgivings in particular. Both women were guests on Seth Meyers’ Thanksgiving episode of “Late Night,” and early on in the interview, admitted that their Thanksgivings have two very different vibes. Fey, being a New Yorker, described a holiday that tests your fortitude just a bit. “New York Thanksgiving, you get up, you stand in the ice cold wind, you look at giant balloons that hopefully are — the wind is blowing them into a sexual position you can laugh about,” Fey detailed. “Go home. You trip on a rat. You have a nice meal.” With that, Poehler began describing an average Thanksgiving in Los Angeles, putting on her best Valley girl voice. “In LA, we do things a little differently,” she joked. “We have turkey, or a turkey substitute, and then we get a smoothie, and then we eat our leftovers on the beach. And it’s different. But it’s fun!” Naturally, Fey immediately joined in on the joke, putting on her own affected voice, and taking the bit even further. “You put all your sides and your turkey in the bowl, and shake it like a salad,” Fey joked. “And then you go, ‘Mm mm mm,’ and you don’t eat it!” Not one to be left out, Meyers also joined in on the joke, though unfortunately, he didn’t use a funny voice to do it. title: Justin Timberlake Refuses to Sing Backstreet Boys Song During ‘Tonight Show’ Mash-Up: ‘Sacrilegious!’
summary: "I do not desire this!" the NSYNC singer protests The post Justin Timberlake Refuses to Sing Backstreet Boys Song During ‘Tonight Show’ Mash-Up: ‘Sacrilegious!’ appeared first on TheWrap .
content: If you were a pop music fan in the early 2000s (particularly if you’re a woman), you likely had some very heated arguments with your friends on one topic in particular: Backstreet Boys vs. NSYNC. You had to be one or the other, and on Thursday night, Justin Timberlake made his allegiances pretty clear. Obviously, he’ll always be Team NSYNC considering, well, he was in the band. But when it came time to actually perform a Backstreet Boys song during his Thanksgiving appearance on “The Tonight Show,” Timberlake jokingly refused. “Oh god,” he said as the music kicked in. “No, no, no, no, no, no, no.” Host Jimmy Fallon took the lead, having no qualms about musically betraying his best friend. As Fallon sang the opening lyrics of “I Want It That Way,” Timberlake ripped his hand from Fallon’s. “I do not desire this!” he said. Still, Fallon pressed on, singing earnestly. “This is sacrilegious, what will the fans say?” Timberlake tried one last time, before happily singing out with his whole chest. Naturally, the audience joined in as well. The number was part of the duo’s “History of Party Songs” bit, in which they sang a roughly 6-minute mashup of popular party songs from over the years, including “This Is How We Do It,” “Brick House,” “Get Low” and more. Surprisingly (and perhaps insultingly), and for reasons unknown, no NSYNC songs made it into the medley of party songs. Not even “Pop” or “Bye Bye Bye.” The post Justin Timberlake Refuses to Sing Backstreet Boys Song During ‘Tonight Show’ Mash-Up: ‘Sacrilegious!’ appeared first on TheWrap .

title: ‘Percy Jackson’ Stars and EPs Break Down That Heartbreaking Death and What’s to Come
summary: The first demigod has fallen The post ‘Percy Jackson’ Stars and EPs Break Down That Heartbreaking Death and What’s to Come appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Note: Major spoilers ahead for Episode 4 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” officially featured its first death of the series this week, and it was just as heartbreaking as fans expected, even as it differed from the books a bit. So, what comes next? In episode 4, Percy (Walker Scobell) and the rest of the quest team find themselves in the junkyard of the gods. Upon their entrance, they wake Talos 1.0, a massive sentry that, while less of a problem than the real Talos, is an exceedingly hard thing to defeat. But, thanks to Tyson (a surprise appearance from Season 2 star Daniel Diemer), the demigods figure out how to shut Talos down. It requires entering the giant robot through its ankle, and hitting a kill switch in its head. In the end, it’s Bianca di Angelo (Olive Abercrombie) who pulls it off. But, as she waves at her new friends in victory, the sentry falls to the ground, and no demigod could survive that, right? Here’s your final spoiler warning, folks. Alas, Bianca doesn’t survive, and in her dying moments, she pledges herself officially to the Hunters of Artemis and tells Percy to watch out for her little brother Nico (Levi Chrisopulos). Nico himself is back at camp, but he certainly feels his sister’s death, and Chrisopulos teases rough times ahead for the young demigod. “I mean, losing a sibling, and not only that, but really, your only family,” he told TheWrap. “Bianca and Nico are literally — they’ve only had each other their whole lives. So I think, you know, if your whole family suddenly died and you entrusted someone else to protect them, that would really take a toll on someone.” Naturally, the entire quest group is devastated watching Bianca fade out, but it’s Thalia Grace (Tamara Smart) who seems to take it hardest in the moment, as she discovers that Bianca used the last of her ambrosia, which heals demigods, on Thalia herself. “I think a lot of the feelings that I was feeling in that moment were deep rooted in the loss that I’ve experienced [in real life], alongside the incredible Olive, who was just — her performance was so beautiful and was so impactful in a way that I think just, it really just changes the tone of the show,” Smart told TheWrap. Disney+ “I think when you have someone like that, really working that hard, it’s very easy to feel genuinely about what you’re experiencing,” she continued. “I felt, as Thalia, it was very easy to grieve Bianca and just feel that loss because it’s so immersive. The whole situation, you’re in the junkyard, you can’t see anything that doesn’t look like junkyard. And we had obviously prepped for the scene, and I think a lot of things that Thalia is experiencing is overwhelming, and guilt, and trauma from her past and her childhood, and I think it’s just entirely overwhelming for her.” Smart is not wrong about the tonal shift of the show. It’s something that the executive producers were “very deliberate” about this season, knowing that their stars and the characters those stars play, as well as the audience, are growing up. “I think that the choice to allow the story, to ask the story to grow up with its characters, and I think to some extent with its audience, was something that felt important,” Jon Steinberg told TheWrap. According to Craig Silverstein, he and his team took their cues from the books, but made sure to still be mindful of younger viewers, and not make the moment too scary. “It was really hard because, if you look at the book, they don’t show her body, and there’s nothing there, and they can’t find her,” Silverstein told TheWrap. “But they’re also very definitive that she’s dead, right? So it’s this really tough thing when you’re rendering that on screen, like, you have to have the body, and so we have to deal with that problem.” “There were many conversations about how she would be laid, and how we could sell that it was clear that she was dead, but also not make it too upsetting, even though it’s very upsetting.” One thing they always knew for sure was the placement of it. Executive producer Dan Shotz noted that they knew from the jump that Bianca’s death would mark the midway point in Season 3, and truly up the stakes. One way they did that was by leaving the audience in near silence as the credits rolled on the episode. “When we got to that end, and you have that big moment, and everybody is crushed, and you are weeping, then when it went into our big theme, it didn’t play,” he explained. “You wanted the audience to be able to sit with this, and deal with the the trauma of that experience.” Don’t worry though, Olive Abercrombie herself wasn’t too shaken up. According to the producers, word from set on that particular filming day was that she “was so thrilled with her own performance, and the ability and the opportunity to do that, that she was actually skipping away at the end of the day.” “I think the actors around her were the ones who were more traumatized by having to perform this,” Shotz said with a laugh. “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” is now streaming on Disney+. The post ‘Percy Jackson’ Stars and EPs Break Down That Heartbreaking Death and What’s to Come appeared first on TheWrap .

title: The 7 Best New Movies on Netflix in November
summary: Including one of the biggest movies of 2026 — and one of the best The post The 7 Best New Movies on Netflix in November appeared first on TheWrap .
content: The end of the year brings plenty of time for streaming, and Netflix has a slate of films coming to the service that will satisfy your holiday desires. This November library contains movies old and new, including one of the best new releases of the year. Here are the seven best new movies streaming on Netflix in November. “Bridesmaids” (Universal Pictures. “Bridesmaids” You can’t go wrong with “Bridesmaids,” one of the defining comedies of the 2010s. Annie Mumolo and Kristen Wiig’s screenplay is razor-sharp with a staggering number of laugh-out-loud moments, while Paul Feig directs an all-timer comedy ensemble. Both of the film’s nominations at the Academy Awards — Best Original Screenplay for Mumolo and Wiig, Best Supporting Actress for Melissa McCarthy — are incredibly well-deserved. Kyle Gallner and Samara Weaving in ‘Carolina Caroline’ (Magnolia Pictures) “Carolina Caroline” Adam Carter Rehmeier’s “Carolina Caroline” is a delightful crime thriller, starring Samara Weaving and Kyle Gallner in a stylish and sexy “Bonnie & Clyde” riff. Rehmeier has been on a strong run this decade, delivering a series of under-the-radar gems like “Snack Shack” and “Dinner in America.” Now’s the perfect time to catch up with his latest. Netflix “Gentle Monster” Léa Seydoux returned to the Cannes Film Festival in 2026 with a duo of films in competition for the Palme d’Or: Arthur Harari’s “The Unknown” and Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster.” Now on Netflix, the latter is a bleak drama about a pianist who makes a shocking discovery after moving to the countryside from Munich. It’s excellently performed by Seydoux, who is becoming one of the most interesting and reliable presences on our screens. “Looper” (TriStar Pictures) “Looper” Before he broke the Internet’s brains with “The Last Jedi” or introduced the world to Benoit Blanc in “Knives Out,” Rian Johnson brought audiences a brilliantly original sci-fi flick in “Looper.” Bruce Willis and Joseph Gordon-Levitt both shine in this crime film about an assassin who kills men sent back in time from the future, only to be confronted by his own older self. “Looper” doesn’t rank among the top of Johnson’s filmography, but this writer/director doesn’t know how to make anything less than fascinating. “Obsession” (Credit: Focus Features) “Obsession” Have you heard of “Obsession”? It only made more than $500 million on a budget of less than $1 million. Curry Barker’s big-screen debut has been the talk of the town in Hollywood this year, and for good reason. Besides its ridiculous box office success, “Obsession” is a well-shot, cleverly scripted and relentlessly scary horror flick that features a remarkable lead performance from Inde Navarrette — and an underratedly great central turn from Michael Johnston, too. “Possible Love” (Joo Jae-bum/Netflix) “Possible Love” Lee Chang-dong doesn’t make movies often, but when he does, you should pay attention. Just look at “Possible Love,” the writer/director’s first film since 2018’s “Burning.” New on Netflix, “Possible Love” is an emotional epic, brilliantly penned by Lee and Oh Jung-mi with a strong quartet of leading performances. “Possible Love” is one of the year’s very best films, something that feels more like you’re peering into people’s lives than watching a narrative drama. “Whiplash” (Sony Pictures Classics) “Whiplash” Damien Chazelle’s “Whiplash” put the filmmaker on the map, and for good reason. It’s an incredible movie about obsession and the relentless pursuit of “greatness,” anchored by Miles Teller and J. K. Simmons giving arguably their career-best performances. This is another of the defining films of the 2010s, and one that still doesn’t miss a beat. The post The 7 Best New Movies on Netflix in November appeared first on TheWrap .

title: BBC Faces Antisemitism Investigation Over Treatment of Jewish Staff
summary: Britain’s independent antisemitism adviser will examine whether employees’ complaints point to a wider institutional problem The post BBC Faces Antisemitism Investigation Over Treatment of Jewish Staff appeared first on TheWrap .
content: The BBC is facing an independent investigation into allegations of antisemitism in its workplace, raising questions about whether one of the world’s most prominent public broadcasters is adequately addressing the concerns of its Jewish employees. Lord John Mann, the British government’s independent adviser on antisemitism, announced Thursday that he was launching the investigation after hearing from Jewish BBC staffers, some of whom he said were afraid to raise concerns about discrimination internally. The investigation comes weeks after a senior BBC executive said there was no evidence of systemic discrimination that would warrant an independent inquiry. It also comes at a sensitive time for the broadcaster, as the British government reviews its governance, funding and public service obligations ahead of the expiration of its Royal Charter at the end of 2027. Mann told BBC Radio 4’s “Today” program Thursday that previous efforts by the corporation to address employees’ concerns had been unsuccessful. His investigation will seek to establish whether the complaints reflect isolated incidents or a broader institutional problem. In a speech Thursday evening, Mann said his decision to intervene stemmed from his belief in the BBC’s future. He argued that marginalizing the voices and perspectives of Jewish employees was incompatible with fair and independent broadcasting. The BBC said in a statement that it takes “any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC.” The broadcaster has introduced mandatory antisemitism training for all employees and encourages staffers to report incidents of discrimination. Earlier this month, BBC Deputy Director General Rhodri Talfan Davies met with representatives of the broadcaster’s Jewish staff network. He also defended the corporation’s existing procedures for handling discrimination complaints, saying they were robust and regularly reviewed, according to The Guardian . The BBC did not immediately respond to TheWrap’s request for comment on whether it intends to cooperate with Mann’s investigation. The meeting followed revelations by Oscar-winning documentary producer Lucie Kon that she had received a £400,000 ($523,852) payout from the BBC after raising allegations of antisemitism. The BBC said it had not upheld Kon’s allegations of antisemitism but acknowledged shortcomings in its treatment of her. Speaking at an event in Manchester on Thursday evening, Mann urged current and former BBC employees to come forward, emphasizing that his investigation was intended to strengthen the broadcaster, Jewish News reported Friday . “What I am repeatedly hearing is people feel cowed and intimidated and frightened, and stay silent and suffer in silence,” he said. Mann has guaranteed anonymity to those who contact him and expects to present his findings to the BBC and the government before Easter. Britain’s Department for Culture, Media and Sport said it would carefully consider Mann’s findings, emphasizing the BBC’s responsibility to ensure that all communities are represented and valued in British public life. The workplace investigation is among several challenges facing the broadcaster. Separately, the BBC is fighting President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit over the editing of his Jan. 6, 2021, speech for a documentary. The corporation has asked a U.S. federal appeals court to intervene , arguing that the Florida court overseeing the case lacks jurisdiction. title: NBC Won’t Air Ad Opposing US Military Aid to Israel Again After Backlash
summary: The network says it is reviewing its approval process after airing the IMEU Policy Project spot during “Saturday Night Live” this week The post NBC Won’t Air Ad Opposing US Military Aid to Israel Again After Backlash appeared first on TheWrap .
content: NBC will not air a commercial opposing U.S. military aid to Israel again after the spot ran during Wednesday’s “Saturday Night Live” Thanksgiving special, drawing backlash from Jewish and pro-Israel advocacy groups. NBCUniversal’s senior management was unaware of the commercial until after it aired, a person familiar with the matter told TheWrap. The company will evaluate its advertising approval process to ensure appropriate levels of review. Wall Street Journal media reporter Joe Flint reported the developments Friday. It’s unclear whether additional airings had been scheduled or whether NBC determined the commercial violated its advertising standards. The IMEU Policy Project did not immediately respond to TheWrap’s request for comment. NBCUniversal’s advertising guidelines , updated in October, state that the company generally accepts political and issue-based advertising from groups with differing viewpoints, provided their claims are factually grounded and fall within the bounds of reasonable debate. NBCU also reserves the right to reject commercials containing graphic or offensive material it deems unsuitable for its programming. The 30-second commercial, titled “Every Three Seconds” and paid for by the pro-Palestinian nonprofit Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, depicts an American girl saving $400 to buy a bicycle before cutting to a Palestinian girl in Gaza who is missing a leg. The narrator claims that the U.S. sends Israel $400 in taxpayer money every three seconds and links that spending to the girl’s injuries. The National Jewish Advocacy Center sent a letter Friday to Mark Marshall, NBCUniversal’s chairman of global advertising and partnerships, questioning what evidence the network relied on to approve the commercial and requesting records related to its broadcast. The Israeli-American Council has also called on the Federal Communications Commission to investigate whether the advertisement complied with its rules, according to Business Insider . The Orthodox Union, meanwhile, criticized NBC for airing a commercial that highlighted Palestinian civilian suffering without acknowledging Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel. The IMEU Policy Project said the advertisement was part of a national campaign urging Americans to contact their congressional representatives to oppose a new military aid agreement with Israel. The existing 10-year, $38 billion military aid agreement expires in 2028. President Donald Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. would end its annual military aid to Israel by the end of this year, although U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee expressed uncertainty Tuesday about whether that timeline would be met. title: Texas Marching Band Raises $350,000 to Stay in New York for Postponed Macy’s Parade
summary: "It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," the Pearland High School marching band director says The post Texas Marching Band Raises $350,000 to Stay in New York for Postponed Macy’s Parade appeared first on TheWrap .
content: A Texas marching band managed to do some serious fundraising after bad weather threatened to ruin their trip to New York City. The Pearland High School marching band was scheduled to perform in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on Thursday, but the day before balloons and floats started roaming the streets it was announced that, for the first time ever, the parade was being pushed to Saturday due to bad weather. Rather than head home, the band and its community shot to work to come up with the $350,000 to extend the stay of the 500-member group. “It’s been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness,” Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band told CBS News . “I started scrambling through that … Can we find a hotel to stay in? Can we get our transportation back? How, at the last second on a holiday weekend, how astronomical are the prices going to be?” He continued: “This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out.” The Pearland community banded together once the news broke Wednesday and by Thursday they had raised hundreds of thousands of dollars to ensure the group could stay. There were a few logistical loopholes – the band had to relocate from their Times Square hotel because it was booked for the weekend, and they’ll bus home because there were no open flights until Monday or Tuesday – but they got the job done. “We are going to make sure you stay there,” Kevin Cole, Pearland’s former mayor, added. “We are going to make sure you get to perform.” Weather was being monitored in the lead-up to the parade, with rules prohibiting the massive balloons from flying in the city if sustained winds surpass 23 mph or if gusts hit 34 mph or more. That led to the decision to delay until Saturday morning. “The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration. Due to the expected severe weather, the 100th March of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, Nov. 28,” Macy’s said in a Wednesday statement via NBC News. “Our team is working through the operational logistics for this change and will share details as they are finalized. We expect the Parade to kick off at 8:30a.m. on Saturday. Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.” The post Texas Marching Band Raises $350,000 to Stay in New York for Postponed Macy’s Parade appeared first on TheWrap .

title: Emma Roberts and Nina Jacobson Talk Fashion, Film and the Art of Building Character at Tory Burch
summary: WrapStyle: Plus, a major exhibition celebrates architect Paul R. Williams at LACMA The post Emma Roberts and Nina Jacobson Talk Fashion, Film and the Art of Building Character at Tory Burch appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Emma Roberts and Nina Jacobson brought together fashion, film and books at Tory Burch’s Rodeo Drive boutique. At LACMA, a major exhibition celebrates Paul R. Williams, the trailblazing architect who helped shape Los Angeles’ midcentury glamour. Miley Cyrus’ bridal style is another reminder that the wedding aisle has become fashion’s newest red carpet. Meanwhile, Sergio Hudson and Fashion Trust U.S. hosted a rooftop dinner in West Hollywood that turned into a late-night dance party. Nina Jacobson and Emma Roberts, both wearing Tory Burch, celebrate The Hunger Games: Sunrise of the Reaping at Tory Burch Rodeo Drive. Source: Tory Burch/BFA Emma Roberts and Nina Jacobson Talk Fashion, Film and the Art of Building Character at Tory Burch Fashion, film and literature converged at the Tory Burch boutique on Rodeo Drive last week, when actress Emma Roberts and producer Nina Jacobson joined writer and producer Karah Preiss for a conversation about the art of book-to-screen adaptations, the power of costume and what it takes to bring beloved literary characters to life. Co-hosted by Belletrist, the book club and reading community founded by Roberts and Preiss, and Lionsgate, the event celebrated the release of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.” Before the conversation, guests mingled over brunch bites, browsing and shopping Tory Burch’s Fall 2026 collection. Naturally, the three women were dressed for the occasion in Tory Burch. Roberts wore a patent leather skirt and cashmere-silk T-shirt with D’Orsay pumps, while Jacobson opted for a suede jacket, pants and purple ribbed tie-neck top. Preiss wore a wool sweater layered over a poplin shirt with a rounded collar, paired with tailored trousers. For Jacobson, who has shepherded Suzanne Collins’ entire “Hunger Games” series from page to screen, the secret to a successful adaptation has been knowing what to leave out. Quoting Billy Ray, the screenwriter of “Sunrise on the Reaping,” she compared the process to sculpting an elephant from stone: Start with a large block and carve away everything that isn’t the elephant. The challenge with the “Hunger Games” films was preserving the emotional power and character relationships while translating internal thoughts into action. “When you’re making a movie, it’s often about subtraction,” she said, noting that the shift from film to television for “Crazy Rich Asians,” which is due to start production next year, offers the opposite opportunity: to expand the world and explore more characters’ lives. Karah Pleiss, Nina Jacobson and Emma Roberts in conversation at Tory Burch Rodeo Drive. Source: Tory Burch/BFA Fashion is an important form of storytelling, particularly in the dystopian world of “The Hunger Games,” where it communicates class, wealth and power before a word of dialogue is uttered. Jacobson said the new film’s visual language takes inspiration from the late 1970s, although the costume department was discouraged from relying on period clichés. In the impoverished District 12, clothing is worn, handed down and repurposed, while the Capitol’s extravagant fashions reflect its excess and privilege. Glenn Close, who plays Drusilla Sickle, was deeply involved in creating her character’s look, collaborating with director Francis Lawrence on the military touches and elaborate wigs. She even used tape to pull back her face for a snatched, surgically enhanced effect rather than relying on prosthetics. “It really ought to be a manifestation of a character from the inside out,” Jacobson said of great costume design. Roberts shared that her two favorite ways of preparing for a role are imagining her character’s wardrobe and building a bookshelf for her. During particularly dark scenes on “American Horror Story,” she realized that reading Chelsea Handler’s “My Horizontal Life” between takes wasn’t exactly helping her stay in character, so she switched to Stephen King. Costume fittings can also be transformative. “I’ll think I have something all figured out, and how I’m going to walk and look and then I go into a fitting, and it gives me so many more ideas,” she said. As a viewer, she also sees how costumes can make or break a story. “When you watch a show or a movie and you’re like, ‘I could be this for Halloween or implement this in my daily life,’ that’s the sweet spot.” Costumes can be just as nostalgic for an actor as they are for viewers, Roberts said, recalling how she finally took home the black Prada boots worn by her character Madison Montgomery in “American Horror Story: Coven,” 13 years after filming, only to find her original socks still stuffed inside. Roberts tries to collect something from each project, such as charms that bring back memories. The conversation also turned to “Love Story,” Ryan Murphy’s series about John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette, whose minimalist 1990s wardrobe has become a fashion obsession. Jacobson addressed the backlash after Murphy shared early photos from the series, revealing just how fiercely audiences felt ownership over Bessette’s style. “We were really hideously dragged at the time, and we were really lucky we were hideously dragged,” she said of the opportunity to course-correct the costumes , hiring Rudy Mance to take over. “But it wasn’t fun at the time and it wasn’t fun for poor Sarah Pidgeon who all of a sudden was having this real life parallel to Carolyn.” Roberts, for her part, said she was so taken with the show’s wardrobe that she went home and questioned everything in her closet. With “Sunrise on the Reaping” inspiring its own fashion moment, Roberts predicted that audiences would dress up to see it, much as they did for “Barbie.” “I feel like going to a movie should be an event,” she said. After all, why leave the costumes onscreen? Julius Shulman portrait of Paul R. Williams, 1952. Source: Getty Research Institute, J. Paul Getty Trust Paul R. Williams, an Architect of L.A. Glamour, Gets His Due at LACMA The glamour of midcentury Los Angeles owes much to architect Paul R. Williams. Just look at the Beverly Hills Hotel, where his signature pink-and-green palette and iconic script logo helped create the look of Hollywood leisure. Known as the “architect to the stars,” Williams designed homes for Frank Sinatra, Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz, and Barbara Stanwyck. His work helped popularize the elegant indoor-outdoor living that became synonymous with Southern California. He also left his mark on legendary Hollywood gathering places, including the Beverly Hills Hotel’s Polo Lounge and Chasen’s restaurant, with its plush red leather booths. Paul R. Williams, El Mirador Hotel alterations and additions, Palm Springs, 1952, jointly owned by the Getty Research Institute and the University of Southern California School of Architecture. Source: Della M. Williams Trust But there was much more to Williams, as a fantastic new exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art makes clear. “Paul R. Williams: Architect for Living,” on view through May 31, 2027, explores the extraordinary breadth of his career, from glamorous homes and hotels to churches, schools, hospitals, public housing and commercial buildings, many of which served Black communities in Los Angeles. Paul R. Williams, Beverly Hills Hotel, Crescent Wing, 1949, photo by Julius Shulman, 1949. Source: Getty Research Institute, J. Paul Getty Trust Born in Los Angeles in 1894, Williams became the first Black member of the American Institute of Architects in 1923, overcoming racial barriers to build one of the most prolific architectural practices of his generation, with thousands of projects to his credit. He famously learned to draw upside down so white clients who might have been uncomfortable sitting next to him could view his plans from across a desk. He also made a habit of touring construction sites with his hands in his pockets to spare clients the discomfort of deciding whether to shake hands with a Black man, as his granddaughter Karen Elyse Hudson recalls in a short film featured in the exhibition. He designed homes in exclusive neighborhoods where segregation rules prevented him from living. Gallery view of Paul R. Williams: Architect for Living. Source: Museum Associates/LACMA/Jonathan J. Urban Curated by Staci Steinberger, the exhibition includes archival drawings, photos and personal effects, including a customized green piano from the modernist home Williams designed for himself and his wife, Stella, in the early 1950s. The color recalls the signature palette of the Beverly Hills Hotel, while the home’s sweeping staircase has the same flair that distinguished his celebrity commissions. (Museum visitors can watch an amusing clip of Frank Sinatra giving a tour of his Williams-designed Beverly Hills bachelor pad on Edward R. Murrow’s “Person to Person” TV show in 1956.) Another section showcases his work on the Beverly Hills Hotel and the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles, the El Mirador in Palm Springs and the futuristic La Concha Motel in Las Vegas, with its dramatic concrete shell. Williams’ work in Las Vegas also included efforts to develop an integrated casino in the then-segregated city, a project that was never realized. Paul R. Williams residence of Frank Sinatra, Beverly Hills (dining room), 1955–56, jointly owned by the Getty Research Institute and the University of Southern California School of Architecture. Source: Della M. Williams Trust The exhibition is equally devoted to Williams’ commitment to Black Los Angeles. Early commissions such as the Second Baptist Church and the 28th Street YMCA helped establish his practice, while his monumental headquarters for Golden State Mutual Life Insurance became a symbol of Black economic achievement. His residential work ranged from lavish estates to modest homes and public housing, underscoring his belief that good design should serve people across social and economic lines. “You could be born in a Williams-designed hospital, attend a Williams-designed school, get married in a Williams-designed church,” Steinberger explained during the exhibition’s press preview. She emphasized how the architect shaped everyday life in Los Angeles through his conservative modern style, axial layouts and complex curves that guided movement through spaces. His influence extended to the city’s shopping culture, too. At Saks Fifth Avenue in Beverly Hills, he created several intimate, residential-style salons, including the Pompeian Room, a swimwear department decorated in cool green with classical detailing. Paul R. Williams, Saks Fifth Avenue, Beverly Hills (Pompeian Room), 1937–40. Source: Maynard Parker, 1940, Maynard Parker Collection, The Huntington Among those attending the preview was Williams’ granddaughter and biographer Karen Elyse Hudson, who has spent decades researching, documenting and preserving his legacy, helping make this exhibition and others possible. The LACMA show is part of a larger exploration of Williams’ legacy, with concurrent exhibitions at the USC Fisher Museum of Art and the Getty Research Institute. Together, they offer a more complete portrait of an architect whose influence extended far beyond Hollywood’s most glamorous addresses. Paul R. Williams: Architect for Living , on view through May 31, 2027, at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, 5905 Wilshire Blvd., Los Angeles . lacma.org . Paul R. Williams, First African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church of Los Angeles, West Adams, Los Angeles (sanctuary), 1960–69, jointly owned by the Getty Research Institute and the University of Southern California School of Architecture. Source: Della M. Williams Trust Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando wear Saint Laurent at their wedding. Source: Saint Laurent Miley Cyrus’ Wedding a Fashion Windfall for Saint Laurent The wedding aisle continues to rival the red carpet as a powerful showcase for luxury fashion houses, with Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando’s nuptials delivering a windfall for Saint Laurent. Morando, the drummer for L.A. rock band Liily and a songwriter and producer who has collaborated with Cyrus on several albums, has been her partner since 2021. Cyrus, a longtime devotee of the French fashion house, wore an elegant, long-sleeved ivory silk gown with a dramatic plunging back, designed by Anthony Vaccarello, who departed Saint Laurent in October after a decade as creative director. Her look was classic, with just enough sex appeal, and accessorized with matching pointed silk heels. Morando also committed to the label, wearing a single-breasted tuxedo jacket and trousers in grain de poudre wool, a cotton poplin shirt, silk satin tie, grained leather Lewis sneakers and SL 970 sunglasses. From her pumps to his shoppable-now sneakers and shades, the couple’s wedding at Frank Sinatra’s former Palm Springs estate really was a head-to-toe Saint Laurent moment. As I’ve written before , luxury brands have zeroed in on Hollywood brides, using their weddings to make fashion statements that can generate as much attention as an awards-season placement, if not more. It’s a golden opportunity because while red carpets can feel like an endless merry-go-round of designer looks, a wedding dress carries more emotional weight, and the photos have a much longer shelf life. It’s also notable that the Cyrus-Morando photos were distributed by Saint Laurent and that she tagged the brand on Instagram several times. Which raises the question: Will we ever see those Taylor Swift Dior wedding looks? Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando wear Saint Laurent at their wedding. Source: Saint Laurent Inga Beckham, Sergio Hudson and Sheryl Lee Ralph attend the Fashion Trust U.S. x Sergio Hudson Dinner at PUBLIC West Hollywood, Nov. 20, 2026. Source: Getty Sergio Hudson and Fashion Trust U.S. Turn Up the Heat in West Hollywood It was a chilly night on the verdant, park-like rooftop of the new PUBLIC hotel in West Hollywood, but the LALO Tequila was flowing, helping keep the starry crowd warm as designer Sergio Hudson and Fashion Trust U.S. hosted a dinner celebrating his Fall 2026 collection. Brandy, Sheryl Lee Ralph, Jeannie Mai, Michaela Jaé Rodriguez, Karen Pittman and Cookie Johnson were among the guests who dressed up and stepped out for Friday night’s event, which continued well into the night. Celebrity makeup artist Sir John took a turn as DJ, and the dancing eventually moved downstairs to the bar. Also in the mix were stylist and “The Look of Michelle Obama” author Meredith Koop, dancer Ezra Sosa and “Million Dollar Listing” cast member Tracy Tutor. Brandy Norwood and Sergio Hudson. Source: Getty Hudson, whose sharp tailoring and unapologetic glamour have made him a favorite of Michelle Obama, Beyoncé and Kamala Harris, among others, has been busy expanding his reach beyond the red carpet. His latest venture is an adorable collaboration with OshKosh B’gosh, developed in partnership with Harlem’s Fashion Row. The collection marks his first foray into children’s wear, bringing his signature bold color and sophistication to the brand’s pint-sized denim and overalls. Sergio Hudson, Meredith Koop and Sarween Salih. Source: Getty The dinner also celebrated the mission of Fashion Trust U.S., founded by Tania Fares to support emerging American designers through grants, mentorship and industry access. title: The Real Cost of Semafor’s $100,000 Speaker Booker Conflict | Analysis
summary: An undisclosed payment to a Paramount adviser puts the credibility behind Semafor's lucrative events business at risk The post The Real Cost of Semafor’s $100,000 Speaker Booker Conflict | Analysis appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Semafor says its journalists are insulated from commercial influence, but its $100,000 consulting deal with Jason Miller exposed a problem in the other direction: Reporters covering one of his corporate clients weren’t told their employer was paying him. For a publisher that has built a profitable events business around independent journalism, that information gap threatens something far harder to price than a speaker-booking fee: the credibility that makes its reporting — and the events built around it — valuable. The company paid Scipio Strategic, a firm run by longtime Trump adviser Miller, $100,000 in April to help recruit guests for its World Economy summit. Paramount Skydance paid Miller’s separate firm, SHW Partners, $420,000 in March and June, according to financial records first reported by The Washington Post . Semafor reporters covering Paramount’s pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery considered Miller part of the story given that he was paid by David Ellison’s company, but didn’t know their employer was also paying him, as the outlet’s media editor later acknowledged. The disclosure failure carries particular weight for a news organization founded partly on the promise of greater transparency. Semafor has promoted its journalism as a way to rebuild audience trust by distinguishing facts from analysis and opinion. Its journalists may have remained free from business-side interference, but they weren’t informed about a financial relationship relevant to their coverage. That put the credibility behind their work — as well as its journalism-driven events — at risk. And, as Kevin Baron, who previously oversaw events at Politico and Defense One, put it: “Credibility is the currency.” There’s no evidence Miller influenced Semafor’s reporting. But the controversy revealed a gap in how commercial information reached the newsroom. Veteran media reporter Paul Farhi said the arrangement raised concerns regardless of whether Miller was used as a reporting source. “It gives the appearance of a conflict, even if the newsroom isn’t quoting him,” Farhi told TheWrap. He called the arrangement “a bad look for Semafor” and said journalists should have been informed about the consulting relationships. The financial stakes are substantial for Semafor. Events generated roughly half the company’s $40 million in 2025 revenue, helping it report its first profitable year. The company, founded in 2022 by CEO Justin Smith and editor-in-chief Ben Smith, raised another $30 million in January at a $330 million valuation, with plans to expand its newsroom and events business. That success has made securing influential guests a commercial priority. But it also creates a tension for publishers increasingly reliant on live events: The political relationships that help attract prominent speakers can become liabilities when they overlap with newsroom coverage. A Semafor spokesperson told TheWrap that the company’s business team oversees clearly labeled sponsored sessions, while journalists retain control over editorial interviews without sponsor involvement or commercial restrictions. The company said it doesn’t pay speakers. Max Tani, media editor at Semafor, and FIFA President Gianni Infantino appear on stage during Semafor World Economy 2026. (Credit: Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images) An unusual arrangement Baron said he was familiar with consultants helping recruit speakers for private executive gatherings but hadn’t encountered this particular arrangement in his own editorial events work. Farhi similarly said he’d never heard of such a deal, though neither claimed to know how common comparable conflicts were across the industry. Baron cautioned against assuming that paying an outside consultant meant the resulting journalism was compromised. Still, he said he’d expect a financial relationship to be disclosed when relevant to newsroom coverage, while acknowledging that journalists don’t need to know about every business-side hire. Semafor maintains that using outside consultants is standard industry practice. In addition to Miller, the company worked with former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway and Democratic strategist Adrienne Elrod to help recruit event guests. Semafor’s own journalists have defended its independence. In a column Sunday , Semafor media editor Max Tani wrote that he’d never been pressured to soften coverage for commercial reasons. He described prospective guests withdrawing after Semafor refused requests to avoid difficult questions, including about the Iran war. But Tani also acknowledged the reputational consequences of the consulting arrangements. He wrote that hiring the political advisers had fueled conspiracy theories that undermined Semafor’s reporting and undercut its message of transparency. His assessment illustrates why editorial independence alone doesn’t resolve the problem. A newsroom’s journalism can remain uncompromised while undisclosed financial relationships create doubts about its work. A fine line In an internal staff note reported by the Post, Ben Smith acknowledged that some people in the newsroom and events team knew about the consulting arrangements, but most did not. Following the revelations, Semafor added disclosures to 11 articles and newsletters involving Miller, Conway and Elrod and pledged to disclose relevant relationships going forward. The company said Miller wasn’t quoted or mentioned in its Washington coverage during his contract, though two business stories referred to him in passing. The business rationale for hiring politically connected bookers, meanwhile, isn’t difficult to understand. Semafor’s World Economy summit attracted more than 30 official partners this year. The company also promotes an invitation-only Principals program featuring private receptions, roundtables and curated networking opportunities. Those offerings illustrate the commercial value of bringing influential people together, though they don’t establish that sponsors can purchase access to government officials or influence editorial interviews. Baron said sponsors of Washington policy conferences often want to reach particular lawmakers, regulators or government officials rather than simply generate brand exposure. Journalists, meanwhile, want prominent guests because their interviews can produce news. When Baron organized editorial events, his guiding principle was straightforward: “We had to make news on stage.” Farhi described a market driven by competition for prominent guests and intermediaries who know whom to call. “They’re selling the same thing lobbyists in Washington are — perceived influence with important and powerful people,” he said. Hiring politically connected consultants can therefore make commercial sense. But the consultants may also have clients whose activities are being scrutinized by the same news organizations paying them. Semafor hasn’t identified which guests Miller helped recruit. For Semafor, the challenge isn’t necessarily building a stronger wall between its newsroom and events business. It’s determining what information needs to cross that wall. As the company expands its profitable events operation, the relationships of its paid consultants could become increasingly relevant to journalists covering its other clients. The business side shouldn’t dictate coverage, but editors need enough information to identify potential conflicts before they become public controversies. The $100,000 payment to Miller was a business expense. The credibility behind Semafor’s journalism is an asset that could take considerably longer to rebuild if damaged. title: UK Backs Bill to Protect Journalists From Abusive Lawsuits
summary: Press freedom advocates say the proposed safeguards don't go far enough The post UK Backs Bill to Protect Journalists From Abusive Lawsuits appeared first on TheWrap .
content: The British government on Friday backed legislation aimed at preventing wealthy individuals and organizations from using costly lawsuits to intimidate journalists and suppress investigative reporting. The bill would expand legal protections for journalists and whistleblowers in England and Wales beyond cases involving economic crime. However, press freedom advocates warn that reporters could still incur substantial legal expenses before qualifying for those protections. Existing safeguards against strategic lawsuits against public participation, commonly known as SLAPPs, were introduced in 2023. The new legislation would extend those measures to investigations into sexual misconduct and other matters of public interest. Similar concerns exist in the U.S., where 40 states and Washington, D.C., had enacted anti-SLAPP legislation as of August, but no equivalent federal law exists . “No one should be able to use their wealth or influence to silence legitimate scrutiny,” Sarah Sackman, Britain’s minister for courts and legal services, said in a statement Friday. Under the legislation, judges could dismiss lawsuits identified as SLAPPs early in proceedings if plaintiffs cannot demonstrate that their claims are likely to succeed. Defendants would also generally be shielded from paying plaintiffs’ legal costs in such cases, even if they lose. The UK Anti-SLAPP Coalition has called for changes to the bill, arguing that its early dismissal mechanism is too complicated and sets too high a legal threshold, according to a House of Commons research briefing published Wednesday. “At present, the early dismissal process in the Bill is incredibly complex,” National Union of Journalists General Secretary Laura Davison said in a statement Monday. The British government’s announcement comes amid an ongoing legal battle between the BBC and President Trump in the U.S. The broadcaster recently asked a federal appeals court to toss Trump’s defamation lawsuit over its editing of his Jan. 6, 2021, speech. The bill, introduced by Conservative lawmaker John Whittingdale, received its second reading in the House of Commons Friday and must clear further legislative stages before becoming law. title: Bill Maher Believes Trump Doesn’t ‘Appreciate’ How ‘Fair’ He Has Been to Him
summary: “Not every idea he had was bad,” the “Real Time” host tells Piers Morgan The post Bill Maher Believes Trump Doesn’t ‘Appreciate’ How ‘Fair’ He Has Been to Him appeared first on TheWrap .
content: “Real Time” host Bill Maher believes President Trump does not appreciate just how “fair” he has been to him over the course of his two presidential terms. Maher appeared this week as the first guest on the first episode of Piers Morgan’s new interview series with TIME Studios. Throughout the wide-ranging, 41-minute conversation, Morgan spoke with Maher about everything from his early career as an up-and-coming comedian to his potential future retirement. At one point, Maher even touched on his controversial White House dinners with Trump. In October, Maher’s second dinner with Trump was followed just days later by a 1,300-word social media rant from the president in which he lambasted the “Real Time” host, calling him a “complete and total loser.” In his interview with Morgan, Maher seemed unfazed by Trump’s rant. “He did the same thing after the first dinner,” Maher said. “It’s amazing to me that he didn’t see that the same thing was going to happen, especially since we had texted in between the dinners and he had said to me, ‘I get it, you know, I’m not going to try to convert you. This is about two people who don’t agree, who can still talk.'” “Kid Rock invited me to the first one. [Trump] invited me to the second one,” Maher added of his White House dinners. “I brought Kid Rock with me as a friend because he brought me to the first one, and I brought Stephen A. Smith, who I now see was back at the White House, which is great. You know, I think I did a good thing. Now, he has a Black friend.” Maher said Trump has followed “the same pattern” after both of their dinners. “We have dinner. Yes, we talk. He’s awesome in person. I’ve rarely met anyone who is easier to talk to,” the comedian explained. “You can be exactly how you are with him. That dinner lasted four hours. I mean, we had a good time, and then I got back to my job, and that’s when the heartache began.” “I gotta do my job, and he doesn’t really appreciate that I have been fair to him,” Maher argued. “It has not all been, ‘Everything is terrible.’ That’s what most people do. They hate him so much that they also have to hate the ballroom or whatever, and I don’t hate the ballroom.” The “Real Time” host went on to say that he believes Trump’s biggest problem has not been that all of his ideas are wrong but that he entrusts the wrong people to carry them out. “Not every idea he had was bad,” Maher said. “The problem is most of the ways he went about doing it went too far or went off the tracks or were helmed by idiots, because that’s who he has in the administration. Not competent people. People who are loyal, because that’s the only thing he cares about.” “You have morons trying to carry out ideas that, in some cases, were good ideas,” he concluded. title: Gayle King to Step Away From ‘CBS Mornings’ After Son-in-Law’s Death at 45
summary: The morning show anchor will break from the program for one week after Virgil Miller’s “courageous battle with cancer” The post Gayle King to Step Away From ‘CBS Mornings’ After Son-in-Law’s Death at 45 appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Gayle King will step away from “CBS Mornings” following the death of her son-in-law Virgil Miller to cancer. “Mornings Family – I’m sorry to be delivering this sad news,” “CBS Mornings” executive producer Jon Tower said in a memo to staff. He continued saying that “over the Thanksgiving holiday” Virgil lost his life after a “courageous battle with cancer.” Tower added: “Our thoughts right now are with her daughter, and their two beautiful children. We’re respecting the family and giving them privacy as they get through this difficult time.” The memo added that King planned to step away from the show for the next week to “help with family matters.” She plans to return to the show beginning on Dec. 7. Miller married King’s daughter Kirby Bumpus back in December 2020. The couple wed at Bumpus’ godmother Oprah Winfrey’s home. Miller is survived by his wife and their two children, son Luca, 5, and daughter Grayson, 2. Miller spent 10 years as chief of staff for former U.S. Rep. Cedric Richmond on Capitol Hill in Washington D.C. and in 2019 moved on to join the Akin Gump law firm to serve as a senior policy advisor. King praised her late son-in-law often on social media. Back in 2022, in a post both about Miller’s birthday and his and Bumpus’ son’s birthday, she called him “my fav son-in-law” and a “great husband to fav daughter @kirbybump & best dad to fav grandson.” The post Gayle King to Step Away From ‘CBS Mornings’ After Son-in-Law’s Death at 45 appeared first on TheWrap .
